CVP-A18:0: The respiratory diverticulum is an endoderm-lined outgrowth of the ventral foregut in week 4.
Endoderm forms respiratory epithelium and glands. Surrounding splanchnic mesoderm forms connective tissue, smooth muscle and cartilage.
Before partition, the early bud communicates with the foregut.
CVP-A18:1: Primary bronchial buds form the right and left main bronchi.
Secondary bronchi supply lobes (three right, two left). Tertiary bronchi supply bronchopulmonary segments.
A branching conducting airway can exist before a thin, vascular exchange surface develops.
CVP-A18:2: Course sequence: pseudoglandular → canalicular → terminal-sac → alveolar. Alveolar development continues after birth.
Capillary apposition and thinner distal epithelium shorten the diffusion path.
Type I cells provide the thin exchange surface. Type II cells produce surfactant.
CVP-A18:resp26-origin: The week-4 ventral foregut outgrowth has an endodermal lining and splanchnic mesodermal support.
Tracheoesophageal partition leaves a ventral airway and a dorsal esophagus.
A proximal blind pouch stops a feeding tube. A distal tracheoesophageal fistula can still let air into the stomach.
CVP-A18:resp26-maturation: Canalicular development adds distal luminal enlargement and vascular association after pseudoglandular branching. Around 28 weeks falls in the terminal-sac phase in the course timeline.
Type II cells lower surface tension through surfactant. Deficiency raises the work of inflation and favors collapse.
Distal structure, vascular contact and surfactant capacity matter more than a stage label alone.
CVP-A18:resp26-cavities: Lung buds expand into pericardioperitoneal canals. Splanchnic mesoderm forms visceral pleura; somatic mesoderm forms parietal pleura.
Pleuropericardial folds carry the phrenic nerves and separate the pleural and pericardial cavities.
Pleuroperitoneal folds close the connection between thorax and abdomen.
CVP-A18:resp26-clinical: Oligohydramnios or compression from herniated abdominal contents can restrict lung growth and cause hypoplasia. Agenesis means failure to form.
A blind proximal esophagus with a distal airway connection combines atresia and fistula.
Distinguish reduced lung size from surfactant deficiency. A single gestational age or flotation finding cannot settle clinical viability or live birth.
CVP-A19:0: Visceral pleura covers the lung and extends into fissures. Parietal pleura lines the enclosing thoracic surfaces.
The layers are continuous at the lung root. The normal potential space between them contains a thin serous fluid film.
Costal pleura lines the ribs; mediastinal pleura faces the mediastinum; diaphragmatic pleura covers the diaphragm; cervical pleura extends above the clavicle.
CVP-A19:1: Intercostal nerves carry pain from costal and peripheral diaphragmatic parietal pleura.
Phrenic afferents carry pain from mediastinal and central diaphragmatic parietal pleura.
Visceral pleura receives autonomic fibers through the pulmonary plexus and senses stretch; ordinary sharp pain is chiefly parietal.
CVP-A19:2: The costodiaphragmatic recess forms between costal and diaphragmatic parietal pleura. Deep inspiration makes the lung occupy more of it.
At the midaxillary line, the resting lung edge is near rib 8 and the pleural reflection near rib 10.
The costomediastinal recess lies anteriorly at the costal-to-mediastinal reflection.
CVP-A19:resp26-surface: At the midclavicular, midaxillary and posterior lines, lung borders are approximately 6–8–10 and pleural borders 8–10–12.
The apex and cervical pleura project above the clavicle. The right horizontal fissure follows the fourth costal cartilage anteriorly.
Listen for right middle-lobe sounds anteriorly around ribs 4–6 and lower-lobe sounds mainly posteriorly.
CVP-A19:resp26-layers: Visceral pleura follows the fissures. Mediastinal parietal pleura covers the lateral mediastinum.
Fluid occupies the pleural potential space and can collect in the dependent costodiaphragmatic recess when upright.
A thin fluid interface allows sliding and couples the moving chest wall to the lung.
CVP-A19:resp26-sensory: Costal and peripheral diaphragmatic pleura → intercostal nerves → localized thoracic pain.
Mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura → phrenic nerve (C3–C5) → possible shoulder referral through convergent spinal input.
Movement of inflamed pleural surfaces explains pain that worsens with deep breathing.
CVP-A19:resp26-clinical: Pleural air breaks lung–chest wall coupling and permits recoil. A tension mechanism traps air and progressively raises pleural pressure.
Dependent fluid can blunt the costophrenic angle. Inflamed pleural surfaces can produce a friction rub.
The main intercostal bundle runs under the rib above, explaining the anatomical rationale for access above the rib below; clinical fluid access is selected with ultrasound.
CVP-A20:0: Septum transversum → central tendon; dorsal esophageal mesentery → crura.
Pleuroperitoneal folds close posterolateral channels; body-wall muscle contributes the peripheral rim.
Knowing the origin of the central tendon does not explain the origin of the crura or muscular edge.
CVP-A20:1: Pleuroperitoneal folds close posterolateral thoracoabdominal communications, while pleuropericardial folds separate pleural and pericardial spaces.
With a posterolateral defect, abdominal organs can move into the thorax and restrict prenatal lung growth.
Keep the normal aortic, esophageal and caval routes separate from a pathological open canal.
CVP-A20:2: The developing diaphragm starts near cervical levels and descends while retaining phrenic connections from C3–C5.
Phrenic nerves provide motor supply and central pleural sensation. Intercostal nerves carry sensation from peripheral diaphragmatic pleura.
The phrenic nerve’s long thoracic course reflects this developmental descent.
CVP-A20:resp26-contributions: In a section, find the posterior vertebral column and aorta before tracing the four components.
The anterior septum transversum supplies central tendon; dorsal esophageal mesentery supplies crura.
Pleuroperitoneal folds close the posterolateral gaps, and body-wall muscle grows in around the periphery.
CVP-A20:resp26-descent: T8: IVC through central tendon. T10: esophagus and vagal trunks through muscle. T12: aorta and thoracic duct behind the diaphragm.
C3–C5 phrenic fibers descend with the diaphragm. Central pleural irritation may refer to the shoulder.
Peripheral diaphragmatic pleura uses intercostal sensory supply. Opening levels are not fixed dome boundaries.
CVP-A20:resp26-hernia: A posterolateral Bochdalek-type gap permits abdominal viscera to enter the thorax and can produce pulmonary hypoplasia.
A hiatal hernia uses the esophageal opening. Eventration is an elevated but continuous dome.
Hypoplasia is reduced lung growth; mediastinal displacement describes position.
CVP-A21:0: Autonomic motor targets include myocardium, smooth muscle and glands. Somatic motor axons supply skeletal muscle, including diaphragm via phrenic nerves.
Cardiac sympathetic drive increases rate and conduction. Vagal drive slows SA rate and AV conduction.
A signal traveling from a thoracic organ toward the CNS is a visceral afferent.
CVP-A21:1: Primary spinal cardiac pain afferent cell bodies lie in upper thoracic dorsal root ganglia. Sympathetic chain ganglia are motor relays.
Convergence of cardiac and somatic input explains referred chest or medial-arm pain, without requiring arm injury.
Contrast upper thoracic cardiac referral with C3–C5 phrenic referral to the shoulder.
CVP-A21:2: CN X carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to terminal ganglia near or within thoracic organs. The final postganglionic axons are short.
Vagal output slows SA firing and AV conduction; airway parasympathetic output promotes constriction and secretion.
Vagal sensory fibers carry signals toward the brainstem. Preganglionic motor fibers travel toward the organ.
CVP-A21:resp26-organization: Brain and spinal cord form the CNS. Peripheral nerves and ganglia belong to the PNS.
Dorsal root ganglia contain pseudounipolar primary sensory neurons. Spinal somatic motor neurons are multipolar.
An axon conducts output away from the soma. Somatic motor output goes to skeletal muscle.
CVP-A21:resp26-spinal: Dorsal root = sensory, with DRG. Ventral root = motor. The joined spinal nerve and both rami are mixed.
Myelinated preganglionic sympathetics enter the trunk through white rami at T1–L2.
Unmyelinated postganglionic axons return through gray rami at all spinal levels. Organ branches can leave the trunk directly.
CVP-A21:resp26-sympathetic: Cardiac sympathetic preganglionic somata lie in upper thoracic intermediolateral cord. Their axons travel via ventral roots and white rami to cervical or upper thoracic chain ganglia.
Postganglionic cardiopulmonary branches reach the cardiac plexus and increase SA rate, AV conduction and contractility.
Many abdominopelvic splanchnic fibers are still preganglionic when they pass through the chain.
CVP-A21:resp26-vagal: Cardiac vagal preganglionic neurons originate in medullary nuclei including nucleus ambiguus and the dorsal motor nucleus.
They synapse near or within the target, giving a long preganglionic and short postganglionic path.
Vagal effects are strongest at the SA and AV nodes. Direct ventricular inotropic influence is comparatively limited.
CVP-A21:resp26-afferents: Cardiac pain afferents can accompany sympathetics yet have their primary soma in a DRG and enter via the dorsal root.
Convergence with somatic signals explains referred pain. Vagal afferents carry physiological reflex input to the brainstem.
Classify a fiber by direction and role even when sensory and motor axons share a nerve bundle.
CVP-A22:cardinal: Anterior cardinal veins drain the cranial embryo. Each joins its posterior counterpart to form a common cardinal vein entering the sinus venosus.
The cross-connection forms the left brachiocephalic vein; right anterior cardinal below it plus right common cardinal forms the SVC.
Persistent left SVC often drains through the coronary sinus.
CVP-A22:ivc: IVC from top to bottom: hepatic = right vitelline-derived channel; prerenal = right subcardinal; renal = anastomotic; postrenal = right supracardinal.
Bilateral persistence of infrarenal channels can duplicate the IVC.
Failed continuity toward the hepatic segment can divert return through the azygos system.
CVP-A22:fetal-veins: Cardinal veins drain the embryo, vitelline veins the yolk sac and developing gut, and umbilical veins the placenta.
Left umbilical vein brings placental blood in; ductus venosus bypasses part of hepatic circulation toward the IVC.
After birth they become ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum, respectively.
CVP-A22:0: Classify embryonic veins by what they drain: embryo → cardinal, yolk sac → vitelline, placenta → umbilical.
Umbilical venous blood is relatively oxygenated. Direction of flow determines whether a vessel is a vein.
CVP-A22:1: The left brachiocephalic vein is a cross-connection directing left-sided flow to the right SVC.
The usual left heartward cardinal segment regresses. A persistent left SVC can enlarge the coronary sinus.
CVP-A22:2: Fetal route: placenta → left umbilical vein → liver or ductus venosus → IVC → right atrium.
Placental flow stops at birth; portal drainage from gut to liver remains.
CVP-A23:heart-review: Looping changes chamber position; septation establishes separate chambers; outflow development connects them to the great vessels.
Trace the actual opening and use the pressure gradient to predict flow direction.
The foramen ovale flap can close functionally when left atrial pressure rises after birth, before anatomical fusion.
CVP-A23:lung-review: Foregut partition failure can create a tracheoesophageal fistula. Surfactant deficiency destabilizes distal units.
Posterolateral diaphragmatic defects can allow herniated viscera to restrict lung growth.
Use the case clue: abnormal feeding route, unstable immature alveoli, or small lung next to herniated organs.
CVP-A23:0: Pleura versus pericardium → pleuropericardial membranes. Pleura versus peritoneum → pleuroperitoneal folds.
CVP-A23:1: A distal tracheoesophageal connection can deliver air to the stomach; a proximal blind pouch blocks swallowing.
A diaphragm defect allows movement of organs between cavities, rather than a link between two epithelial lumina.
CVP-A23:2: A formed lung bud does not establish adequate surface area, capillary contact or surfactant.
Hypoplasia reduces tissue formed; surfactant deficiency destabilizes distal airspaces.
CVP-P15:hemodynamic-case: CO = HR × SV. MAP − RAP ≈ CO × SVR. Check units when converting mL/min to L/min.
A fall in stroke volume can lower cardiac output even if heart rate is unchanged. Higher SVR can partly maintain pressure despite low flow.
Trace the initiating change before the compensatory response.
CVP-P15:operating-point: At steady state, cardiac output equals venous return at the intersection of the two curves.
Increased contractility lifts the cardiac curve. Increased stressed volume raises mean systemic filling pressure and shifts the venous-return intercept.
Venous return = (mean systemic filling pressure − right atrial pressure) / resistance to venous return. Resistance changes the slope.
CVP-P15:0: Acute volume loss lowers venous return, preload and stroke volume.
Reflex tachycardia, increased contractility, venoconstriction and arteriolar constriction can occur while cardiac output is still low.
CVP-P15:1: Doubling resistance at the same pressure difference halves flow. A rise in downstream pressure can reduce flow even at unchanged upstream pressure.
CVP-P15:2: Low arterial pressure can reflect low cardiac output, low resistance or both.
Use filling, heart rate, peripheral temperature and any direct flow evidence to distinguish the disturbance from compensation.
CVP-P22:0: Alveolar ventilation = respiratory rate × (tidal volume − dead-space volume). Minute ventilation = rate × tidal volume.
At 10 breaths/min with a tidal volume of 600 mL and dead space of 150 mL, minute ventilation is 6 L/min and alveolar ventilation is 4.5 L/min.
Equal minute ventilation can give lower alveolar ventilation if breaths are smaller and more frequent.
CVP-P22:1: Anatomical dead space is the conducting airway volume. Alveolar dead space is ventilation reaching alveoli with little or no perfusion.
Physiological dead space includes both components. More dead space at the same rate and tidal volume lowers effective alveolar ventilation.
CVP-P22:2: At constant CO₂ production, PaCO₂ is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation. Doubling effective ventilation approximately halves PaCO₂.
More dead space at fixed minute ventilation raises PaCO₂. If CO₂ production and effective ventilation rise proportionally, PaCO₂ stays about the same.
CVP-P23:0: Gases diffuse down their own partial-pressure gradients. Use the difference between compartments, not their ratio.
Equal partial pressures give no net diffusion. If blood partial pressure is higher, net diffusion is toward the alveolus.
Compare gradients separately from surface area, thickness and the gas’s diffusion coefficient.
CVP-P23:1: Fick’s law: transfer is proportional to surface area, diffusion coefficient and partial-pressure difference, and inversely proportional to barrier thickness.
At fixed other factors, doubling area doubles transfer; doubling both area and thickness leaves it unchanged.
Fibrosis thickens the barrier; emphysema can remove exchange area.
CVP-P23:2: CO₂ has a higher effective diffusivity than O₂ largely because it is more soluble.
A higher diffusion coefficient does not mean the observed transfer of both gases changes by the same amount. Their driving gradients also differ.
CVP-P24:0: Pulmonary flow goes from right ventricle to lungs to left atrium.
In steady state, pulmonary and systemic flow are essentially equal. The pulmonary circuit operates at much lower pressure because it has lower resistance.
CVP-P24:1: Low local alveolar PO₂ constricts nearby pulmonary arterioles and diverts blood away from the poorly ventilated region.
Many systemic vessels instead dilate in response to local hypoxia.
Widespread alveolar hypoxia can raise total pulmonary vascular resistance.
CVP-P24:2: Gravity raises vascular hydrostatic pressure toward the base in an upright lung, tending to increase dependent perfusion.
When alveolar pressure exceeds pressures inside surrounding vessels, they can compress and flow can be minimal or absent.
The same total pulmonary blood flow can have different regional distributions.
CVP-P25:0: Most oxygen is hemoglobin-bound. PaO₂ measures dissolved oxygen tension; saturation is the fraction of available hemoglobin sites occupied.
Halving hemoglobin at the same saturation and PaO₂ roughly halves the bound oxygen component. A normal PaO₂ does not guarantee normal oxygen content.
CVP-P25:1: Increased CO₂, H⁺, temperature or 2,3-BPG shifts the O₂–hemoglobin curve right and decreases affinity.
At a fixed PO₂ a right shift lowers saturation and facilitates unloading. Cooling shifts left and increases binding.
CVP-P25:2: Most blood CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate. Carbonic anhydrase speeds conversion of CO₂ and water in red cells.
In systemic capillaries, bicarbonate exits and chloride enters the erythrocyte. Some CO₂ binds globin as carbaminohemoglobin.
CVP-P26:oxygen-levels: Hypoxemia means low arterial PO₂. Tissue hypoxia can arise from low oxygen content, reduced blood flow or impaired oxygen use with normal PaO₂.
Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content. Hemoglobin concentration and saturation dominate content.
CVP-P26:gradient: A–a difference = calculated alveolar PO₂ − measured arterial PO₂. Use PAO₂ ≈ FIO₂ × (PB − PH₂O) − PaCO₂/R.
On room air at sea level with PaCO₂ 40 and R 0.8, PAO₂ is about 100 mmHg. PaO₂ 60 gives an A–a difference near 40 mmHg.
Hypoventilation or low inspired PO₂ usually preserves the difference. V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation and shunt usually widen it.
CVP-P26:oxygen-response: Low V/Q and diffusion limitation often improve with higher inspired oxygen.
In a true right-to-left shunt, some blood bypasses ventilated alveoli, so the oxygen response is comparatively limited.
Interpret oxygen response with the A–a difference and case details.
CVP-P26:0: Low PaO₂, low hemoglobin content, low tissue flow and impaired tissue utilization can all limit oxygen availability by different mechanisms.
Normal PaO₂ can coexist with hypoxia from anemia or low flow.
CVP-P26:1: Hypoventilation raises PaCO₂ and lowers calculated PAO₂. PaO₂ can fall while the A–a difference stays relatively normal.
Low PaO₂ despite adequate PAO₂ widens the difference and points to impaired transfer or mixing.
CVP-P26:2: Exercise can shorten capillary transit and expose diffusion limitation when the barrier is thickened or area reduced.
A shunt is a flow path past an unventilated region. It differs from incomplete equilibration across a ventilated barrier.
CVP-P27:gravity: Both ventilation and perfusion tend to be greater at the base upright, but perfusion rises more steeply. Apex V/Q is higher.
High V/Q means relatively higher alveolar O₂ and lower CO₂. It does not mean high absolute ventilation.
Calculate ventilation ÷ perfusion for each region before comparing.
CVP-P27:extremes: V/Q = 0 means perfusion without ventilation: the shunt limit.
V/Q approaching infinity means ventilation without perfusion: alveolar dead space.
The former returns poorly oxygenated blood; the latter wastes ventilation.
CVP-P27:0: A low V/Q unit has some ventilation but relatively too much blood flow. Its alveolar oxygen is lower and CO₂ higher.
Supplemental oxygen can reach partially ventilated low-V/Q units. It cannot directly oxygenate a completely unventilated shunt unit.
CVP-P27:1: A perfusion obstruction with intact airflow creates alveolar dead space. More minute ventilation may be needed to maintain useful ventilation.
An airway obstruction with intact blood flow produces the opposite limiting V/Q pattern.
CVP-P27:2: Well-ventilated units already near the hemoglobin saturation plateau can add little extra oxygen content.
Mix blood by oxygen content and flow weighting, rather than averaging alveolar PO₂ or regional ratios.
CVP-P28:control: Sensor → brainstem integration → respiratory muscles → change in alveolar ventilation.
Rising PaCO₂ drives more ventilation, which tends to lower PaCO₂. That opposing response is negative feedback.
Shallow breaths can increase minute ventilation without proportionally increasing alveolar ventilation.
CVP-P28:chemoreceptors: Central chemoreceptors respond mainly to CO₂-driven pH changes in brain extracellular fluid and CSF.
Peripheral chemoreceptors, especially carotid bodies, sense low PaO₂ and respond to arterial CO₂ and pH.
Low PaO₂ is different from low oxygen content due to anemia.
CVP-P28:reflexes: Large lung inflation stimulates vagal stretch afferents that can inhibit inspiration.
Airway irritation can cause cough. Pulmonary congestion can activate afferents associated with rapid shallow breathing.
Identify the initiating mechanical or chemical stimulus before choosing the receptor.
CVP-P28:0: CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier and generates H⁺ in CSF and brain extracellular fluid. Acute acidification increases ventilatory drive.
Bicarbonate compensation alters the response to chronic CO₂ retention. Arterial H⁺ crosses less freely than CO₂.
CVP-P28:1: At altitude, barometric pressure falls while oxygen fraction remains about 21%, reducing arterial PO₂.
Peripheral chemoreceptors drive hyperventilation. The resulting fall in PaCO₂ can partly oppose the response centrally.
CVP-P28:2: Metabolic acidosis stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors and increases ventilation.
Lowering PaCO₂ reduces the respiratory contribution to acidity, partially compensating for the primary metabolic disturbance.
MOL-20:synthesis: Phosphoglucomutase makes G1P from G6P. UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase activates G1P to UDP-glucose.
Glycogenin supplies the primer. Synthase extends α(1→4) chains; branching enzyme forms α(1→6) junctions and adds nonreducing ends.
MOL-20:mobilization: Phosphorylase uses inorganic phosphate at α(1→4) bonds to release G1P. It stops near a branch.
Debranching transferase moves residues, then α(1→6)-glucosidase releases one free glucose from the branch point.
MOL-20:regulation: Insulin favors dephosphorylation, activating synthase and reducing phosphorylase activity.
Hepatic glucagon activates Gs → cAMP → PKA, favoring phosphorylase activation and synthase inhibition.
Muscle mobilizes glycogen in response to epinephrine, Ca²⁺ and AMP during contraction.
MOL-20:disease: Von Gierke: hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase defect blocks glucose export from both glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis.
McArdle: muscle phosphorylase defect causes exercise intolerance. Pompe: lysosomal acid α-glucosidase defect causes lysosomal storage.
Branching enzyme defects leave long, poorly soluble glycogen chains.
MOL-20:0: Glycogen has one reducing end associated with glycogenin and many nonreducing ends.
α(1→4) extends chains, α(1→6) creates branches. More nonreducing ends allow faster parallel synthesis and breakdown.
MOL-20:1: Phosphorylase performs phosphorolysis of straight α(1→4) chains, producing G1P.
Debranching glucosidase hydrolyzes α(1→6) bonds to release free glucose. Phosphorylase then resumes.
MOL-20:2: Both liver and muscle mobilize glycogen to G6P.
Liver glucose-6-phosphatase permits export of free glucose. Muscle lacks that route and uses G6P locally for glycolysis.
MOL-21:oxidative: Each G6P oxidized yields 2 NADPH, CO₂ and ribulose-5-phosphate; ATP is not a direct product.
The two oxidative dehydrogenases reduce NADP⁺. NADPH feeds back on G6PD, while NADP⁺ availability supports flux.
MOL-21:rearrangement: Transketolase transfers two carbons and requires TPP; transaldolase transfers three.
Reversible exchanges connect pentoses to fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. They can make ribose from glycolytic intermediates without producing NADPH.
MOL-21:red-cells: Red cells rely on PPP NADPH to regenerate reduced glutathione via glutathione reductase.
In G6PD deficiency, oxidant exposure can denature hemoglobin and injure membranes. Heinz bodies and bite cells reflect that injury.
MOL-21:0: The cytosolic oxidative PPP makes NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and redox defense.
Ribose supplies nucleotide carbon and can also come from the reversible nonoxidative reactions. NADPH and NADH have distinct major roles.
MOL-21:1: Low G6PD activity → limited NADPH → less GSH regeneration → peroxide damage and possible hemolysis under oxidant stress.
This is failure of redox defense, not a direct block in ATP-generating glycolysis.
MOL-21:2: Transketolase moves two carbons using TPP. Transaldolase moves three.
Rearrangements conserve total carbon and produce neither CO₂ nor NADPH. They can run toward or away from pentoses.
MOL-22:formation: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to H₂O₂. Hydrogen peroxide is reactive but is not a radical.
Reduced iron plus peroxide can generate hydroxyl radicals. Nitric oxide synthase makes NO from arginine; NO can react with superoxide to make peroxynitrite.
MOL-22:defense: Glutathione peroxidase uses GSH to detoxify peroxide, yielding GSSG. Glutathione reductase spends NADPH to regenerate GSH.
Catalase decomposes hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen. It does not directly use the glutathione cycle.
MOL-22:injury: Phagocyte NADPH oxidase deliberately produces superoxide during the respiratory burst. Its deficiency impairs microbial killing.
Myeloperoxidase uses peroxide and chloride to make hypochlorous acid downstream.
G6PD deficiency instead weakens antioxidant defense against oxidants.
MOL-22:0: Superoxide and hydroxyl are radicals. Peroxide is a nonradical ROS.
Peroxide can still generate highly reactive hydroxyl radicals near reduced transition metals.
MOL-22:1: SOD removes superoxide; catalase and glutathione peroxidase remove peroxide.
Glutathione reductase targets oxidized glutathione rather than peroxide.
MOL-22:2: Peroxidase consumes GSH during detoxification. Reductase replenishes GSH using NADPH.
A recycling defect can limit peroxide clearance even when peroxidase is present.
MOL-23:fructose: Fructokinase forms fructose-1-phosphate. Aldolase B splits it to DHAP and glyceraldehyde.
Fructokinase deficiency causes benign fructosuria. Aldolase B deficiency traps phosphate in fructose-1-phosphate, impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
MOL-23:galactose: Galactokinase forms galactose-1-phosphate. GALT acts on that phosphorylated substrate.
GALT deficiency can produce systemic illness with galactose-1-phosphate accumulation. Galactokinase deficiency favors galactitol-related cataracts.
MOL-23:other-sugars: Brush-border lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose. Unabsorbed lactose causes luminal osmosis and fermentation.
Mannose enters glycolysis as F6P. Aldose reductase makes sorbitol from glucose or galactitol from galactose.
MOL-23:0: Fructose-1-phosphate accumulation means fructokinase worked and points downstream to aldolase B.
Loss of fructokinase prevents formation of the phosphate-trapping intermediate.
MOL-23:1: Lactase deficiency leaves lactose in the intestinal lumen, causing bloating and osmotic diarrhea.
Galactose enzyme defects occur after absorption. Cataracts or systemic neonatal liver findings help distinguish the downstream blocks.
MOL-23:2: Aldose reductase consumes NADPH to reduce glucose to sorbitol.
Sorbitol dehydrogenase uses NAD⁺ to oxidize sorbitol to fructose, producing NADH. Slow second-step flux can allow sorbitol accumulation.
MOL-24:oxidation: Cytosolic ADH converts ethanol to acetaldehyde; mitochondrial ALDH converts acetaldehyde to acetate. Each reduces NAD⁺ to NADH.
The carbon stays two-carbon. Poor aldehyde clearance increases acetaldehyde even when ADH still works.
MOL-24:redox: Excess NADH pushes pyruvate toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate, limiting gluconeogenesis.
A high NADH ratio also favors triglyceride accumulation. Fasting makes hypoglycemia more likely when glycogen is already depleted.
MOL-24:0: ADH produces acetaldehyde; ALDH removes it by forming acetate.
If acetaldehyde accumulates, distinguish increased formation from impaired removal. Acetate can be activated to acetyl-CoA.
MOL-24:1: High NADH drives lactate dehydrogenase toward lactate and regenerates NAD⁺.
Lactate can rise from a hepatic redox shift even without an initiating tissue oxygen-delivery failure.
MOL-24:2: CYP2E1 is an inducible microsomal ethanol oxidation route that uses oxygen and NADPH and can generate ROS.
ADH uses NAD⁺. Competing substrates at ADH can slow generation of another alcohol’s downstream metabolites.
MOL-25:energy-vitamins: B₁ supplies TPP for α-ketoacid decarboxylation and transketolase. B₂ supplies FMN/FAD; B₃ supplies NAD⁺/NADP⁺; B₅ supplies coenzyme A.
Pellagra classically causes dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia. Angular cheilitis can occur with riboflavin deficiency.
MOL-25:amino-and-one-carbon: PLP supports transamination and decarboxylation; biotin transfers activated CO₂; folate carries one-carbon units.
B₁₂ supports methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Elevated methylmalonic acid and neurologic findings favor B₁₂ over folate deficiency.
MOL-25:vitamin-c: Vitamin C maintains reduced iron for collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases.
Deficiency weakens connective tissue, causing capillary fragility and poor healing. Vitamin K-related bleeding instead involves defective clotting protein activation.
MOL-25:0: TPP is required at the early decarboxylation step of pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate and branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenases.
Transketolase also uses TPP but transfers two carbons without α-ketoacid decarboxylation.
MOL-25:1: Riboflavin yields FMN/FAD, which can transfer one or two electrons. Niacin yields NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, which accept a hydride.
NADH mainly links oxidation to ATP generation; NADPH mainly supports reductive synthesis and antioxidant defense.
MOL-25:2: Folate and B₁₂ deficiency can both cause megaloblastosis and elevated homocysteine.
Methylmalonic acid rises with impaired B₁₂-dependent mutase activity. Neurologic signs also favor B₁₂ deficiency.
MOL-26:a-d: 11-cis-retinal supports vision. Retinoic acid regulates transcription and differentiation.
Liver converts vitamin D to 25-hydroxyvitamin D; kidney forms active calcitriol, which increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.
MOL-26:e-k: Vitamin E interrupts lipid peroxidation in membranes. Vitamin K enables γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S.
γ-Carboxylation supports calcium-dependent binding to phospholipid. Warfarin interferes with vitamin K recycling.
MOL-26:0: Vitamin C deficiency causes bleeding through weak collagen and vessel fragility.
Vitamin K deficiency impairs γ-carboxylation of coagulation proteins. Similar symptoms can have different biochemical mechanisms.
MOL-26:1: The liver produces 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the usual status marker. The kidney produces active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
Calcitriol acts through a nuclear receptor and promotes intestinal mineral absorption.
MOL-26:2: Vitamin A: vision and gene regulation. Vitamin E: membrane lipid antioxidant. Vitamin K: calcium-binding protein modification.
A shared fat-soluble classification does not imply the same cellular function.
MOL-27:information-review: DNA and RNA are synthesized 5′→3′ from antiparallel templates. RNA matches the coding strand with U in place of T.
Ribosomes read mRNA 5′→3′ and synthesize peptides from N to C terminus.
MOL-27:structure-review: Side-chain charge, hydrophobic packing and active-site contacts can affect folding or function.
Negatively charged GAGs attract counterions and water. Hydrated matrix resists compression; collagen primarily reinforces against tension.
MOL-27:0: DNA polymerase adds to a 3′ hydroxyl, so product grows 5′→3′.
For a template printed 5′→3′, reverse the complement before reporting the product 5′→3′.
MOL-27:1: A site accepts aminoacyl-tRNA, P site holds peptidyl-tRNA before transfer, E site releases empty tRNA.
After transfer the growing chain is on A-site tRNA until translocation. Initiator tRNA starts in P.
MOL-27:2: GAG acidic groups attract cations and water, helping hydrated matrix resist compression.
Hyaluronan is nonsulfated. Negative charge does not require every GAG to be sulfated.
MOL-28:carbon-review: Early fasting uses liver glycogen; gluconeogenesis becomes more important as glycogen falls.

MOL-28:redox-review: NADH carries electrons from fuel oxidation toward pathways such as mitochondrial electron transport.
